senses.gloss:
ātmajñāna
(‘Self-knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
It is अज्ञान or इग्नोरन्चे of the आत्मन्, the सोउल् or the Self, that leads one to the bondage of transmigration. आत्मज्ञान or knowledge of the Self, a direct experience of its real nature, obtained through proper sādhanā or spiritual practice, leads to लिबेरतिओन्.
See also ĀTMAN.

Ātmaprabodha Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a small Upaniṣad belonging to the Ṛgveda. The first part is in prose and the rest in verses.
The prose version appears like a condensation of the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad and deals with the supremacy of नारायण and the अष्टाक्षरी (eight-syllabled) मन्त्र.
The rest of the text describes the subjective experience of the jīvanmukta or the liberated being. He has transcended māyā and has realized his identity with the inmost Self. Hence he is beyond the three guṇas and the codes of conduct that bind the ignorant ones. He is ever pure infinite चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and the spirit sought after by the scriptures. All the beings and all the objects of च्रेअतिओन् exist in him even as the bubbles and the waves exist in the ocean. Being ever blissful in nature, no sorrow or suffering will ever touch him. Unfortunately the ignorant people of the world are not aware of their true nature even as the owl is not aware of the brilliant light of the sun.

ātma-māyā
(‘inherent mysterious power’)
------------------------------------------
Lord Śrī कृष्ण while describing his descent into the human form uses this word (vide Bhagavadgītā 4.6). Though he is unborn, eternal and the Lord of all beings, he takes recourse to his ‘prakṛti’ and incarnates himself through ‘ātma-māyā,’ to re-establish and preserve धर्म or righteousness, by destroying the wicked and protecting the good. प्रकृति comprising the three guṇas, सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्, is the basic matrix out of which the whole universe is evolved. It is also called māyā which is variously interpreted as इल्लुसिओन्, illusory or mysterious power and so on. The इन्चर्नतिओन् of God is not like the rebirth of ordinary jīvas or beings who are forced into birth and suffering due to their past कर्म or deeds. He does it out of his free will exercising his mysterious power, which is inherent in Him. This is ‘ātma-māyā.’
See also MĀYĀ.

ātmasamarpaṇa
(‘self-offering’)
------------------------------------------
Ahirbudhnya Saṁhitā is an important text of the Pāñcarātra school of Vaiṣṇava आगमस्. According to it, union of the jīvātman with परमात्मन् is the ultimate goal of life. This can be achieved either through ‘ātmasamarpaṇa’ (also called ‘hṛdyāga’) or through ‘yoga.’ meditation on God in the form of some of his powers as deities (as for instance, the सुदर्शन-चक्र, the discus-weapon of विष्णु) with appropriate mantras culminating in total self-offering or self-abnegation is ‘ātma-samarpaṇa.’ ‘Yoga’ is very similar to the process taught by पतञ्जलि in his Yogasūtras.
See also AHIRBUDHNYA-SAṀHITĀ.

ātmāśrayatva
(‘[fallacy of] self-dependence’)
------------------------------------------
Indian philosophical systems have recognised ‘tarka’ or ratiocination as an important aspect of the mental process which helps us to determine the truth and to counter the arguments of the opponents. The latter is a necessary component of the former.
While countering the arguments of the opponents, the fallacies in their arguments have to be pointed out. Five such fallacies have been listed: ātmāśraya (self-dependence), अन्योन्याश्रय (mutual dependence), चक्रक (circle), अनवस्था (vicious infinite) and pramāṇa-bādhitār-thaka-prasaṅga (contradictory experience).
Ātmāśrayatva, the first of these, has been defined as that undesirable state in which something is dependent only on itself. This can happen in three different ways depending upon whether we are trying to explain ‘utpatti’ or origination, ‘vṛtti’ or functioning and ‘jñapti’ or know-ledge.
If X is the product of X, then X, the cause could not be present at the instant of time before the one at which X the product came into existence. The principle of causality requires that the cause should precede the product in time. Hence to say that X is the product of the same X is a fallacy.
If X is a function of X, then the cause X must have a larger extension than the function X. But here, being the same thing, the two are coextensive. Hence, to say that X is a function of X (which is identical with the cause X) is a fallacy.
If X is not different from the knowing of X, then, it would be a product of the constituents of knowing and hence be different from X, which is obviously a fallacy.
In all these cases, that which is sought to be proved, depends upon the very same object, and hence a fallacy.

Ātmopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
A small Upaniṣad belonging to the Atharvaveda with just three sections in prose, it deals with three kinds of ‘puruṣas’ or beings, called ‘ātmā’. The first is the physical body comprising the various limbs and subject to birth and death. It is the ‘bāhyātmā’ or the outer आत्मन्. The second, called ‘antarātmā,’ the inner आत्मन्, is the मिन्द् composed of the sūkṣma-bhūtas or the subtle elements and responsible for the functions of the senses as also the various states like thinking, feeling and willing. The third and the last is the ‘paramātmā’ or the ‘puruṣa,’ the Supreme Self or the Person. He is the true Self who is subtler than the subtlest, beyond all change and destruction, the eternally pure witness of all, the infinite, the indestructible.
Some texts contain an additional part in verses numbering 31, describing this आत्मन्-ब्रह्मन्, the unreal nature of the manifested world and the state of लिबेरतिओन् of the emancipated being.

ātmahatyā
(‘suicide’)
------------------------------------------
Ātmahatyā or सुइचिदे has been consi-dered a great sin by the धर्मशास्त्रस् (vide पराशर Smṛti 4.1 and 2; Yama Smṛti 20 and 21). Though it was prescribed as the ultimate punishment for sinners of most heinous crimes (Manusmṛti 11.90, 91; Gautama Dharmasūtras 23.1), it was also disapproved by other writers.
However, it was permitted as a religious act under certain circumstances like a वानप्रस्थ (forest hermit) suffering from incurable diseases and unable to perform his duties, an old man incapable of taking care of himself due to serious old-age decrepitude or illness beyond cure, a householder who has fulfilled all his duties and obligations and has no desire to live and so on.
Such suicides were committed in various ways such as ड़स्तिन्ग् unto death, महाप्रस्थान (See MAHĀPRASTHĀNA for details.), drowning oneself at the त्रिवेणी in प्रयाग (modern Allahabad in Uttar Pradesh) or burning oneself in the fire prepared out of cowdung-cakes.

Ātmabodha
(‘Knowledge of the Self’)
------------------------------------------
Śaṅkara (A. D. 788-820), the doyen of Advaita Vedānta, has composed three types of works: bhāṣyas, prakaraṇas and stotras. The bhāṣyas are his commentaries on the प्रस्थानत्रय (the three basic works of Vedānta viz., उपनिषद्स्, Brahmasūtras and Bhagavadgītā). The stotras are devotional hymns. The prakaraṇas are elementary treatises on Advaita philosophy. Out of nearly 40 prakaraṇas attributed to him Ātmabodha is one of the smaller works. It consists of 68 verses.
As the very name suggests, the work deals with Self-knowledge. After describing briefly the qualifications of an aspirant for मोक्ष, the work proceeds to assert that only ज्ञान (knowledge) can give मोक्ष (liberation) directly, even as it is the fire that is directly responsible for cooking ड़ोओद्. This is followed by a descrip-tion of the world as ‘mithyā’ or transient. Then comes an analysis of the three śarīras (bodies) and the five kośas (sheaths) to prove that the आत्मन् is different from all these. The process of meditation on the आत्मन् comprising the three well-known steps of śravaṇa (hearing), मनन (reflection) and निदिध्यासन (meditation) comes next. It ends with the description of the identity of the जीव (individual सोउल्) with ब्रह्मन् (Supreme Self), and the state of a liberated सोउल्.

ātmānātma-viveka
(‘discrimination between the Self and the non-Self’)
------------------------------------------
The Vedānta system of Indian philo-sophy considers the ब्रह्मन्/Ātman Principle as the only or the Supreme Reality. All other things, perceived or unperceived, are its manifestations, or, ever subservient to it. The primary purpose of life is to realize this Reality as our true Self. But, all efforts at doing so are being negated by our inordinate attachment to our body-मिन्द् complex. Hence this attachment is to be attenuated and ultimately got rid of by sādhana-catuṣṭaya or the fourfold discipline. आत्मानात्म-विवेक heads this list. It consists in separation (viveka) of the आत्मन् (Self) from all that is अनात्मन् (not-Self). The body, the sense-organs, the vital airs, the मिन्द्, the intellect, the egoity—none of these is the आत्मन् and hence fit to be brushed aside. Such discrimination and logical thinking gradually leads to the next higher modes of sādhanā and ultimately to the direct experience of the आत्मन्.
See also SĀDHANA-CATUṢṬAYA and VIVEKA.

ātman
(‘[the Self which is] the essence or the principle of life [or, which] pervades [everything]’)
------------------------------------------
The phenomena of birth and death have always mystified man. Whether there is ‘something’ before birth and whether it survives death has been an eternal question haunting human minds. Most of the Indian philosophical systems have accep-ted the existence of such a spirit, generally termed ‘ātman,’ though views about it have varied greatly.
In the early Vedic literature the word ‘ātman’ has rarely been used. Even when used (vide Ṛgveda 1.115.1) it does not seem to have any mystical or metaphysical significance as found in the later literature. From a simple notion of cosmic unity, the word gradually came to represent the entity which is both immanent and transcendent with regard to the cosmos.
The term ‘ātman’ has been derived and defined in various ways: that which animates; that which pervades; that which experiences; that which exists always. A fuller development of the concept is found in the later Vedic literature such as the आरण्यकस् and the उपनिषद्स्. Here, together with the word ‘Brahman’ it has been used to denote the Cosmic Spirit both in its transcendent and in its immanent aspects. However, gradually, the word ‘Brahman’ came to be used much more to indicate the transcendent Reality whereas the term ‘ātman’ was generally confined to the immanent Reality or the individual self.
Descriptions of the nature of the आत्मन् or the सोउल् as given by the various schools of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् differ widely from one another. The Cārvāka (material-istic) schools deny the existence of a permanent सोउल् and attribute चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् to the chemical reactions brought about by the combination of the pañca-bhūtas or the five fundamental elements constituting the world. जैनिस्म् believes in the existence of eternal souls, infinite in number. They possess चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् which is limited in manifestation but capable of evolving to infinite proportions. बुद्धिस्म्, while denying the existence of a permanent सोउल्, accepts the continuity of life which generates the next life as one tree produces another through its seed.
The न्याय system admits of the existence of ‘ātman,’ an eternal सोउल्, different from the body, the senses and the मिन्द्. It is vibhu or all-pervading and has चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, not as integral to it, but as an adventitious attribute brought about by its association with the मिन्द्. It is an agent of action and suffers its consequences. Due to मिथ्या-ज्ञान or false knowledge or इग्नोरन्चे, it allows itself to be swayed by the impulses of राग (attachment), द्वेष (dislike) and मोह (infatuation). Consequently it performs good or bad actions and suffers their results. It attains अपवर्ग or लिबेरतिओन् by tattvajñāna or right knowledge of the Reality. In this state it is freed from all sorrow, suffering and misery. It is a negative state of transcendence of दुःख (pain, suffering) and not a positive state of bliss as some others deem to think. And, the ātmans are infinite in number.
The Vaiśeṣika view is practically identical with that of the न्याय school.
The Sāṅkhya and the योग systems accept the आत्मन् as an indubitable reality, which they call as ‘puruṣa.’ The पुरुष is eternal, pure and all-pervading चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. He gets into the bondage of सṁसार (transmigratory existence) due to aviveka or non-discrimination between himself and प्रकृति (nature). By विवेक-ख्याति or knowledge that distinguishes him from the प्रकृति, the non-self, he recovers his original state of freedom, freedom from pain and suffering. It is not a state of joy or bliss.
These systems also concede that the puruṣas are innumerable.
The views of the Mīmāṁsā school regarding the आत्मन् or the सोउल्, are very similar to those of the preceding four systems mentioned here. The आत्मन् is an eternal, infinite substance which is related to a real body in a real world. It survives death to be able to reap the consequences of its action performed here. चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is not its essence but only an adventitious quality which arises when some conditions are present. There are as many souls as there are individuals. लिबेरतिओन् is obtained by the disinterested performance of obligatory actions, knowledge of the आत्मन् and the wearing out of the karmas accumulated in the past. Total stoppage of rebirth and remaining in a state beyond pleasure and pain is the special charac-teristic of लिबेरतिओन्.
The Vedānta system has branched off into three main schools—Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and द्वैत.
The Advaita school maintains that the आत्मन् is eternal, infinite and is of the nature of pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. It is, in the ultimate analysis, ब्रह्मन् the Absolute Itself. अज्ञान or the इग्नोरन्चे of its real nature has led to its bondage and ज्ञान or knowledge will lead it to लिबेरतिओन्. This is not a state to be attained but the original state itself regained. In this state it will enjoy unalloyed bliss.
The Viśiṣṭādvaita school declares that the आत्मन् or the सोउल्, though eternal, is not vibhu (infinite) but aṇu (atomic) in size. चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is intrinsic to it, though its contraction and expansion are possible. Such souls are infinite in number. They are different from ब्रह्मन् or God, but parts of it. लिबेरतिओन् is attained by भक्ति or devotion to God. In this state the souls become similar to God but not absolutely identical with him.
According to the द्वैत school, the सोउल् is eternal, atomic in size and has चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् as its essence. The souls are innumerable, different from God and from one another too. They are of three classes: those that are bound but may become liberated; those that are eternally confined to transmigratory existence and those that are doomed permanently to the misery of हेल्ल्. लिबेरतिओन् is obtained by knowledge, devotion to विष्णु, and by his grace. It is living in वैकुण्ठ, the world of God, in his eternal presence. Even in the state of लिबेरतिओन् differences among the liberated souls persist.

ātmaguṇa
(virtues [that help in manifesting] the Self’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu social legislators considered the life of man as an integral unit and prescribed several सṁस्कारस् or sacraments to purify him in all aspects. However, these सṁस्कारस् should not be performed mechanically but with due faith so that the eight general virtues called ‘ātmaguṇas’ can be induced in him. They are: sarvabhūtadayā (compassion towards all creatures), kṣānti (forbearance), anasūyatā (absence of jealousy), शौच (purity), anāyāsa (avoiding exertion), मङ्गल (auspiciousness), akārpaṇya (large-heartedness) and aspṛhatā (absence of covetousness).
This list of eight ātmaguṇas differs from author to author. Other virtues included in such lists are: सत्य (truth), ārjava (straightforwardness), दान (giving gifts), अहिṁसा (non-injury), शम (peace of मिन्द्), दम (self-control) and dhṛti (courage).
The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (8.7) has listed eight guṇas or qualities natural to the आत्मन् as follows: He is apahata-pāpmā (free from sins), vijara (free from decrepitude), vimṛtyu (deathless), viśoka (without sorrow), vijighatsa (free from hunger), apipāsa (free from thirst), satyakāma (of unfailing desires), and satyasaṅkalpa (of unfailing will).
